name: Revanchism
summary: Revanchism is the policy of reversing a defeat, above all of winning back territory lost in war. The word dates from France after 1871, where nationalists such as Paul Déroulède's Ligue des Patriotes wanted Alsace-Lorraine back from Germany, by war if need be. The encyclopedia record shows the talk of revanche never became state policy before 1914, so the sources say little beyond that single aim.
scope: French revanchism after the Franco-Prussian War (1870-1914), as the encyclopedia defines the term, with Déroulède and the Ligue des Patriotes as its documented voice. Other countries' revanchist or irredentist movements, and Wikipedia's list of examples, are not used.

furtherReading.title: Alsace-Lorraine (Encyclopedia of Modern Europe)
furtherReading.note: Shows how the lost provinces became the centre of French revanchism.

furtherReading.title: Paul Déroulède, Qui vive? France, quand même! (archive.org)
furtherReading.note: Speeches and notes of the Ligue des Patriotes founder, in French.

keyFigures.name: Paul Déroulède
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Ligue des Patriotes (1882), the leading voice for revanche against Germany

sources.title: Alsace-Lorraine, Encyclopedia of Modern Europe: Europe 1789-1914
sources.author: Laird Boswell and others, via Encyclopedia.com
sources.usedFor: Defines revanchism as the French drive to reconquer Alsace-Lorraine and names the Ligue des Patriotes; says talk of revenge did not become policy.

sources.title: Qui vive? France, quand même! Notes et discours 1883-1910
sources.author: Paul Déroulède
sources.usedFor: Déroulède's speeches on the war of revanche, the Russian alliance, colonies and the plebiscitary republic.

sources.title: The Rhetoric of Revolution and Reality: Boulangism and Mass Politics in France
sources.author: David Lerer, Tufts University honors thesis, 2011
sources.usedFor: Defines revanchism as revenge against Germany for the defeat of 1870-71 and names Déroulède and his League of Patriots as revanchist.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Déroulède calls the million and a half Alsace-Lorrainers handed to Germany 'livrés contre tout droit' and the annexation the cruellest of iniquities, so he treats it as without legal right.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Déroulède argues for a 'guerre de revanche' to recover the lost provinces, a war of justice, honour and interest; the encyclopedia names reconquest of Alsace-Lorraine as revanchism's principal theme.

strong-leader.rationale: Déroulède wants a plebiscitary president chosen by the people, a 'maître' for a Chamber he accuses of disorder and anarchy; the Ligue backed General Boulanger as the strong man for revanche.

direct-votes.rationale: Déroulède holds that there is no democracy where there is no plebiscite or referendum, and calls his doctrines resolutely plebiscitary, though his own programme centres on electing the president and revising the constitution.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Déroulède declares himself more anti-parliamentary than ever and calls the parliamentarians a new aristocracy living on their privileges.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: Déroulède campaigned for the Franco-Russian alliance and welcomed it as ending Germany's domination of France.

missingStatements.text: A country should seek to recover territory it lost in a war.
missingStatements.rationale: Reconquest of the territory lost in the Franco-Prussian War is revanchism's defining aim, in the encyclopedia's account and in Déroulède's own speeches.

quotes.text: For the French, reconquest of Alsace-Lorraine was the principal theme of revanchism (from the French word for revenge).
Si donc la guerre de revanche n'était qu'une guerre
quotes.where: quivive.txt line 1032 (speech on the war of revanche)

notes: Searched: war and territory, alliances, colonies, constitution and plebiscite, the army, decadence and national renewal (Déroulède's Qui vive; the encyclopedia entry). Britannica, Merriam-Webster and Project MUSE refused scripted access (403) and were not used; Rutkoff's Revanche and Revision (1981) and Varley's chapter in Defeat and Memory (2008) were not available open access. Déroulède is one voice of a thin doctrine, so most statements are null and the uncertainty rule is expected to exclude it.
